chapter_title: Two Stories about Flying (Part I: His First Flight & Part II: Black Aeroplane, with 'How to Tell Wild Animals' & 'The Ball Poem')

branches.theme: Part I: His First Flight by Liam O'Flaherty

sub_branches.concept: Paralysis of Fear on the Cliff Edge
details: A young seagull stands terrified on his cliff ledge while his two brothers and sister fly effortlessly.
He fears his wings will not support him over the expansive ocean below.
His parents fly around screaming, upbraiding him, and threatening to let him starve unless he flies.
evidence_or_examples: Parents threatening: 'let him starve on his ledge unless he flew away.'

sub_branches.concept: Hunger as Catalyst and Mastery of Flight
details: Isolated for 24 hours, the young seagull is maddened by hunger watching his mother tear fish on a rock.
The mother flies near holding a piece of fish in her beak but halts just out of reach.
Maddened by hunger, he dives at the fish, falls into space, experiences momentary terror, and then feels his wing feathers cutting through the air.
He lands safely on the green sea, joined by his cheering family.
evidence_or_examples: Mother dangling fish bait; his wings expanding naturally as gravity takes over.

branches.theme: Part II: Black Aeroplane by Frederick Forsyth

details: The narrator flies his old Dakota DS 088 from France to England at 1:30 AM, looking forward to a warm English breakfast.
150 km past Paris, he encounters massive black storm clouds resembling black mountains.
Inside clouds, visibility drops to zero; compass turns round and round, radio dies, and fuel tanks run low.
evidence_or_examples: Dead compass and broken radio contact with Paris Control.

details: A black plane without lights appears alongside him in the storm; its pilot waves and signals him to follow.
The narrator follows like an obedient child for half an hour until fuel is nearly exhausted.
The black plane guides him down through clouds to a safe lit runway.
Upon inquiring at the control tower, the woman officer informs him no other plane was on radar.
evidence_or_examples: Control tower officer statement: 'Another aeroplane? Up there in this storm? No other aeroplanes were flying tonight.'

branches.theme: Poetic Study: How to Tell Wild Animals by Carolyn Wells

details: Provides humorous rules to identify dangerous beasts: Asian Lion (roars as you die); Bengal Tiger (black stripes on yellow ground, eats you); Leopard (spotted hide, leaps continuously); Bear (hugs tightly); Hyena (smiles) vs Crocodile (weeps).
Demonstrates 'poetic license' by altering spellings ('lept', 'dyin') to maintain rhythm and rhyme.
evidence_or_examples: Poetic license lines: 'If he lepes on you again, 'twill do no good to roar with pain, he'll't leap and lep again.'

branches.theme: Poetic Study: The Ball Poem by John Berryman

details: A young boy loses his ball into the harbor; he stands rigid and trembling watching it sink.
The poet refrains from intruding or offering a dime for another ball, noting 'Money is external'.
The boy learns his first fundamental lesson: the 'epistemology of loss'—how to accept loss and take responsibility in a world of possessions.
evidence_or_examples: Line: 'He is learning, well behind his desperate eyes, / The epistemology of loss, how to stand up...'
